notes.meaning: Darius the Mede took over the government of Babylon after the Babylonian empire fell. This took place around 538 BC, near the time when God's people would finally be allowed to return home.

Daniel studied the scrolls of Scripture and read what God had said through the prophet Jeremiah. He realized that the seventy years Jerusalem was meant to lie empty were almost finished. Instead of doing nothing, knowing God's promise moved Daniel to pray.

Daniel gave his full attention to the Lord in serious prayer. He went without food and wore rough sackcloth and ashes, which were traditional signs of deep grief and humility. He knew that asking God for mercy required an honest, humble heart.

Daniel began his prayer by praising the Lord as great and faithful. God always keeps His covenant, which is His sacred promise, and shows loyal love to those who obey Him. Daniel acknowledged that the Lord had never failed His people.

Daniel admitted the deep guilt of his nation using several words for doing wrong. The people had wandered off track, acted corruptly, and openly rebelled against God's clear rules. Even though Daniel had lived a godly life, he counted himself as part of the sinful nation.

The people had ignored the warnings sent through God's prophets. From the highest kings and rulers down to everyday citizens, no one had listened. Their sin was made worse because God had sent loving warnings again and again.

The Lord is completely fair and right in everything He does, while the people of Israel are filled with open shame. Their suffering and exile across distant lands was the direct result of breaking faith with God. True repentance agrees that God's discipline is just.
Shame covered every level of society, including the kings, leaders, and ancestors who led the way in sin. Daniel offered no excuses for their actions. Everyone stood guilty before God.

Even though the people had rebelled, compassion and pardon still belong to God. Daniel looked to the Lord's mercy as the only safe place of hope. God has the right and the heart to forgive those who have failed Him.

The nation had refused to listen to God or follow the lifestyle He laid out for them. He had made His truth plain through the teachings of Moses and the prophets who followed. Ignoring God's spokesmen was the same as turning away from God Himself.

All Israel had broken God's law, so the warnings and solemn curses written long ago in the Law of Moses fell upon them like poured rain. God had told them what would happen if they turned away, and He kept His word. His judgment proved that He takes His covenant seriously.

God did exactly what He warned He would do to the nation and its rulers by bringing terrible ruin on Jerusalem. Nothing as painful as the fall of Jerusalem had ever happened anywhere under heaven. The depth of the punishment reflected how great their spiritual privileges had been.

All the trouble predicted in Moses' teachings had arrived, yet the people had still been slow to pray with honest hearts. True prayer means turning away from wrongdoing and welcoming God's truth. Hard times should push people directly toward the Lord.

The Lord kept watch over the disaster and brought it at the right time, like an alert guard doing his duty. God did nothing evil or unfair, for He is righteous in all His works. The fault lay entirely with the people who would not obey His voice.

Daniel reminded God of how He rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt with great power long ago. That famous rescue revealed God's lasting glory to the world. Daniel pleaded that the God who saved them then would show that same power once again.

Daniel asked God to turn His anger away from Jerusalem and His holy hill of Zion, based on His faithful promises. Surrounding nations were mocking the Jews and their ruined city, which made God look weak in their eyes. Daniel wanted God's honor to be defended among the nations.

Daniel asked God to smile with favor upon the ruined temple. He pleaded for the Lord to act for His own honor and for the sake of the coming Messiah. Restoring the temple would bring light and joy back to God's worship.

Daniel begged God to look with pity on the battered city that bore His holy name. He made it clear that they were asking for help not because they had done anything good, but only because God is so deeply merciful. True prayer always leans on God's grace rather than human merit.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic scholars note that Daniel's prayer of confession closely matches the wording found in the book of Baruch.

notes.meaning: In short, urgent cries, Daniel pleaded with God to listen, forgive, and take action without delay. His greatest concern was that the city and the people were identified with God's own name. He did not want God's reputation to suffer any longer.

While Daniel was still speaking and confessing his sins and the sins of his people, heaven responded. He was pouring out his heart concerning God's holy mountain when help arrived. God was ready to answer even before the prayer was finished.

The angel Gabriel, whom Daniel had seen in an earlier vision, flew swiftly to his side. He arrived around the hour of the late afternoon sacrifice, about three o'clock. Even though the temple altar was destroyed, Daniel still kept time by God's daily schedule of worship.

Gabriel spoke kindly to Daniel and explained why he had been sent. He came to give Daniel the ability to understand God's deeper plan for the future. God wanted His servant to see what lay ahead for his people.

Gabriel revealed that an answer was sent out the very moment Daniel started praying because God loved him dearly. Gabriel told him to pay close attention to the message that followed. God delights in hearing the prayers of those who love Him.

Gabriel announced that seventy sets of seven, meaning 490 years, were set aside for the Jewish people and Jerusalem. During this time, God would deal with rebellion, end sin, make atonement to repair the broken relationship with God, bring in lasting righteousness, complete all prophecy, and consecrate the Most Holy. These blessings pointed toward the full salvation that Jesus Christ would bring.

differ.view: These six goals will reach their complete fulfillment only when Christ returns to establish His earthly kingdom, even though the cross achieved atonement for sin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: These seventy weeks are symbolic periods that reached their climax in the second century BC when the temple was cleansed after the persecution of Antiochus Epiphanes.

notes.meaning: The count began when an official order was issued to rebuild Jerusalem, lasting seven sets of seven plus sixty-two sets of seven until the Anointed Prince arrived. During the early period, the city would be rebuilt with streets and defensive moats, even during dangerous and difficult times. This foretold the coming of the Messiah after a long season of preparation.

differ.view: The countdown begins with the Persian king Artaxerxes giving Nehemiah permission to rebuild Jerusalem's walls around 445 BC, which points directly to Jesus entering Jerusalem as King.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The anointed prince mentioned after the first seven weeks refers to an earlier figure like Cyrus the Great or the high priest Joshua rather than Jesus.

notes.meaning: After the sixty-two sets of seven, the Messiah would be put to death, dying not for Himself but for others. Afterwards, an invading army would destroy the city of Jerusalem and its temple like a raging flood. This was fulfilled when Jesus died on the cross and Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.

differ.view: There is a long pause or gap between the sixty-ninth week and the seventieth week, during which God builds His church before the final seven-year period begins.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The anointed one who was cut off was the Jewish high priest Onias III, who was murdered in 171 BC during the Greek oppression.

notes.meaning: A covenant would be confirmed with many for the final set of seven, and halfway through that period the old sacrifices would be brought to an end. An appalling desecration would strike the temple until total destruction fell upon the destroyer. Through Christ's sacrifice on the cross, the old ceremonial system was finished forever, followed by the ruin of the temple.

differ.view: The one confirming the covenant is Jesus Christ, who confirmed the new covenant through His ministry and ended the need for temple sacrifices by His death on the cross.
The one confirming the covenant is Jesus Christ, who established the covenant of grace and brought an end to Jewish ceremonial rites by offering Himself.
The one who makes the covenant is a future Antichrist, who will sign a seven-year treaty with Israel and break it halfway through by halting sacrifices in a rebuilt temple.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: This verse describes Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who forced a treaty on Hellenistic Jews, stopped temple offerings, and set up a pagan altar to Zeus in 167 BC.
